10          3.      This action for legal malpractice and breach of fiduciary duty arises out the

20

24   substantial, totaling over $1.5 million.

25          4.      In or around January 2018, Plaintiff Rockhill engaged BABC to represent it in a dispute

26   with an entity named Green Gate Services, LLC (“GGS”), a tribal lending entity owned by the Big
27   Lagoon Rancheria, a federally recognized Native American tribe in Humboldt County, California. The
28
                                                           2
                                                   COMPLAINT
                  Case 1:24-cv-06085-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 3 of 33



 1   dispute arose from a contractual relationship in which Rockhill and/or Dan acted as the executive

 2   director of GGS who offered consumer lending programs to the public. Dan is the President of
 3   Rockhill. This dispute ripened into an arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association
 4
     (the “Arbitration”), pursuant to a permissive arbitration provision in the relevant agreement between
 5
     GGS and Rockhill. During the course of the Arbitration, BABC undertook to represent Dan
 6
     individually in addition to Rockhill. BABC also represented Dan Koetting’s brother, Mark Koetting
 7
 8   (“Mark”) individually, and his company Redondo Management, LLC, (“Redondo”) who had a similar

 9   contract with a related tribal entity, Clear Loan Solutions (“CLS”), which was also owned by Big

10   Lagoon Rancheria. Despite the joint legal representation that was provided by Defendants to Dan and
11   Rockhill and to Mark and Redondo in the Arbitration, the business operations of Rockhill and Redondo
12
     were completely distinct from one another. Rockhill worked under contract with GGS, while Redondo
13
     worked under contract with CLS. CLS and GGS are sometimes referred to herein as the “TLEs,” short
14
     for tribal lending entities. BABC unwisely decided to consolidate the claims relating to Mark and
15
16   Redondo with those of Dan and Rockhill in the Arbitration.

17          5.      Despite being licensed outside of California, Defendants practiced law in California for

18   this engagement. The contracts with GGS and CLS provided for enforcement of an arbitration award in
19   the United States District Court for the Northern District of California or Humboldt County Superior
20
     Court. The TLEs initiated the Arbitration in 2018 with a claim filed on or about January 8, 2018 with the
21
     California offices of the American Arbitration Association (“AAA”). It was clear from the outset that in
22
     addition to seeking recovery from alleged conduct of Rockhill, GGS also sought to hold Dan and a
23
24   related company, Rivo Holdings, personally responsible. GGS identified Rockhill, Rivo and Dan as

25   Respondents in their Demand for Arbitration, and requested a hearing to be held in Sacramento,

26   California. Through BABC as its counsel, Rockhill asserted counterclaims against GGS, and Redondo
27   asserted counterclaims against. CLS. Defendants filed a demand for arbitration with the AAA in
28
                                                         3
                                                  COMPLAINT
                  Case 1:24-cv-06085-RMI Document 1 Filed 08/28/24 Page 4 of 33



 1   California, also requesting that the Arbitration be venued in Sacramento, California. In February 2018,

 2   Defendants agreed to mediate the dispute in California with a California-based mediator. In March 2018,
 3   Defendants through Defendant Smith personally met with Plaintiffs in California and attended mediation
 4
     on behalf of Plaintiffs in San Francisco, California. During the Arbitration, Defendants, through Smith,
 5
     traveled to San Diego, California to meet with Dan, and performed legal services in California. Other
 6
     partners of BABC, through pro hac vice admission in March 2019, appeared at proceedings relating to
 7
 8   enforcement of the Arbitration award in the Superior Court of the State of California in Humboldt

 9   County, and later appeared pro hac vice on behalf of Plaintiffs in the California Court of Appeal.

10          6.      Unfortunately for Rockhill and Dan, Defendants’ services in the Arbitration fell far
11   below the standard of care. Rather than properly marshalling and analyzing the evidence and
12
     presenting the strengths and weaknesses of the case to Dan and Rockhill, Defendants instead rushed into
13
     a consolidated and expedited arbitration with insufficient preparation, minimal discovery, no
14
     depositions, no accounting, and no designation of experts. Most critically, Defendants wholly
15
16   underestimated the strength of GGS’ claims while overestimating the value of Rockhill’s defenses and

17   counterclaims, leading to a one-sided, superficial, and disorganized presentation at the Arbitration which

18   was held on September 10-12, 2018. Defendants failed to timely and properly object to evidence, and
19   present the evidence necessary to defend against GGS’ claims and preclude alter ego liability for Dan,
20
     leaving Rockhill subject to a multimillion-dollar adverse judgment, and Dan facing a multimillion-dollar
21
     award that has yet to be finalized and resulted in years of additional post-Arbitration legal proceedings
22
     in California. The highly unfavorable result in the Arbitration, especially the inflated damages and alter
23
24   ego liability for Dan, resulted directly from the myriad errors committed by Defendants. As revealed by

25   the recent appellate decision, JPV I L.P. v. Koetting, 88 Cal.App.5th 172 (2023), Rockhill and Dan face

26   a potential liability of over $11 million plus 5 years or more of accumulated interest, as a proximate
27   result of the negligence of Defendants in connection with the Arbitration. Judgment has been entered
28

 1   against Rockhill and it is anticipated that judgment will be entered against Dan individually in or about

                    Background of the GGS-Rockhill Relationship
13
            13.     In August 2013, Rockhill entered into a Consultant and Independent Contractor and
14
     Agreement (the “GGS Agreement”) with Green Gate Services, LLC, (“GGS”), a tribal lending entity
15
16   (“TLE”) organized under the laws of the federally-recognized Indian Tribe, the Big Lagoon Rancheria

17   (“BLR”) to operate an online consumer lending program. Dan was the President of Rockhill which was

18   owned 50/50 with his business partner, Jairo Perez.
19          14.     This opportunity had been introduced to Dan by his brother Mark, who had already
20

21
     (“Redondo”) with another TLE owned by BLR called Clear Loan Solutions (“CLS”), also to operate a
22

23
24   Redondo, and the consumer lending programs were administered separately as well. The operations of

25   Rockhill and GGS were completely separate and distinct from the operations of Redondo and CLS.

26          15.     Between 2013 and 2017, Rockhill received legal advice regarding the agreement with
27   GGS from Jennifer Galloway, a Florida attorney, who Plaintiffs allege on information and belief was
28

 1   then operating as a solo practitioner in the State of Florida through her professional association, Jennifer

 2   Galloway, P.A. (“Galloway”). Galloway negotiated and participated in drafting the GGS Agreement for
 3   Rockhill. Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that GGS was also represented by counsel in
 4
     negotiating the GGS Agreement.
 5
            16.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that the underlying purpose of the GGS
 6
     Agreement was to create a consumer lending program qualified for sovereign immunity afforded to
 7
 8   BLR. Indian tribes, such as BLR, are allowed to do this via compliance with an “arm of the tribe”

 9   analysis which essentially requires the tribe to pass a tribal lending code, create a TLE wholly owned by

10   the tribe, with the tribe to exercise some control over the TLE and establish a program to ensure
11   compliance with the tribal lending code.
12

13

14
     which were then used to develop and expand the consumer lending business governed by the GGS
15
16   Agreement.

18   managing the day-to-day operations of the consumer lending platform, including marketing, generating
19   leads, underwriting, and loan servicing for and on behalf of GGS. Rockhill arranged for the monies to
20

21
     the call center for Rockhill, handling customer support. GGS did little to directly service the loans. It
22

23
24   land to service the loans, but never did so. Rockhill generated the leads and arranged for affiliates to put

25   up the capital to finance loans made through the consumer lending platform. The GGS Agreement was

26   silent as to which party would own the leads generated by Rockhill and the customer data related to
27   those who took loans through the consumer lending platform.
28

 1          19.     Plaintiffs allege on information and belief that GGS and BLR were charged with

 4
     dollars (or 1.5%) of active loan balances as of the last business day of each month, with the remainder of

24   Agreement and Rockhill’s obligations under that agreement as the relationship with GGS deteriorated
